item.title: IDEA: Inexpensive things to do in Alaska on a cruise
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
If you're used to cruising in the Caribbean, shore excursion prices on your Alaska cruise might surprise you. Want to take a helicopter ride to the top of a glacier to enjoy a dogsled ride? It'll cost upward of $700 per person. Excited about an authentic Alaska fishing experience? That's a more than $400 tour. A nearly three-hour scenic train ride on the White Pass and Yukon Route Railroad starts at more than $150 per traveler. Not only are tours so pricey because Alaska is a remote destination (where it costs more to fly in goods and materials), but also because Alaska is part of the U.S., where wages and tour insurance costs can be higher than in the islands. Plus, many Alaska excursions involve seaplanes, helicopters, specialized boats and other equipment that only add to the price of your onshore experience. For many, an Alaska cruise is a once-in-a-lifetime trip, and many tours are worth the splurge. But you don't have to spend money hand over fist in every port. Whether you're trying to balance your budget with a few cheaper days or you simply don't have the resources to spend big every day of your vacation, you'll want to seek out cheap or free things to do in Alaska's cruise ports. Luckily, you have plenty of options. I know because I've spent many a day exploring independently in Alaska's ports. Plus, I consulted with Alaska's tourism representatives to bring you a comprehensive list of free (and cheap) things to do in Alaska on a cruise. Things to do in Skagway, Alaska, for free and cheap Skagway is known for its gold rush history, but you don't need a pricey tour to immerse yourself in the town's storied past. Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park has four free museums open to visitors, including the Visitor Center Museum (with interactive exhibits), the Moore House Museum (former home of the first family to live in Skagway, with two restored Victorian-era rooms), the Jeff Smiths Parlour Museum (a former bar with a shady past) and the Mascot Saloon Museum (a restored gold rush saloon). If you're fully embracing the old-timey vibe, you'll want to belly up to the bar at the Red Onion Saloon. Once, it was Skagway's signature bordello, but now it's the place to sling back an Alaska-brewed beer or snack on apps and pizzas named after former good-time girls. For a reasonable $20 a person, you can sign up for a Quickie Tour of the venue's supposedly haunted brothel museum. Ghost sightings don't cost extra! One of my favorite things to do in Skagway is stretch my legs on a hike, and there are several trailheads within easy walking distance of your cruise ship. Options include the Upper and Lower Dewey Lake, Reid Falls and Gold Rush Cemetery, and Icy Lake and Upper Reid Falls trails. The National Park Service kindly lists its hikes by distance from Skagway's Historic District, as well as by level of difficulty. No guide is needed, and you don't have to pay to access the trails. Free and cheap things to do in Juneau, Alaska Window shopping is a popular activity along the main streets by Juneau's cruise docks, but you might be tempted to blow your budget on souvenirs. (Look for sales, especially during end-of-season sailings, if you want to buy gifts for less.) Typically, you can pay $60 for an all-day pass up and down Juneau's Goldbelt tram*, or if you're in good shape, you can hike from your ship to the top of the tram on the Mount Roberts Trail for free. I did this hike on my recent Alaska cruise, and while it's not technical, it is steep and can be muddy after a rainstorm. Make lots of noise just in case bears are on the trail. At the top, you can visit the Chilkat Theater to watch a free movie about the region's Tlingit people. If you're too tired to hike back down, you can get a ride back on the tram for $20. However, the Goldbelt tram has been closed since late April 2026 for maintenance. Visitors can still go to the base of the tram to watch Tlingit artists carve totem poles, weave ceremonial robes and perform cultural dances for no charge. Other hikes accessible from your ship include the Gold Creek Flume Trail and the Perseverance Trail. If a stroll through downtown is more your speed, self-guided tours of Juneau come free of charge. The Juneau Voices project features audio installations at 11 spots around town where you can learn about the city through the stories of Native Alaskans. Or grab a map from a tourist welcome center and follow this walking tour to see the city’s highlights. If you prefer to get your history and culture indoors (not a bad plan in Alaska, given the temperamental climate), Juneau offers a few museums with modest admission fees that are worth checking out. The Juneau-Douglas City Museum offers a mix of permanent and temporary exhibits on the area's history and art. Admission is $7, but you might need a cab if you're not up for a 20-minute walk. The museum also runs a free walking tour of the Alaska State Capitol Building. Also, a 20-minute walk from the port is the Alaska State Museum, where you can learn about the cultures of the Tlingit, Haida and Tsimshian peoples. Admission is $14. For more information on Native Alaskans and their cultures, visit the Sealaska Heritage Institute's Walter Soboleff Building ($10 admission) and its gift shop, which features local art. Don't miss the signature totem pole and handcrafted clan house. If you’re keen for a scenic uphill walk, head up Basin Road to the Last Chance Mining Museum ($5) to learn about the gold rush in a historic mining building. *At the time of writing, Goldbelt tram is closed but has plans to reopen soon. Check availability and prices before you plan. Cheap and free things to do in Ketchikan, Alaska, from a cruise ship Ketchikan is best known for its Creek Street Historic District, built on a wooden boardwalk above the salmon-filled Ketchikan Creek. Stroll for free by its historic buildings, shops and restaurants, or pay $10 to stop into Dolly’s House for a glimpse into the city’s former red-light district. Not far from Creek Street, the Tongass Historical Museum and Totem Heritage Center immerses you in the area’s history for a modest $6 fee (children and military are free). From there, you can embark on a self-guided, 1 1/2-mile Ketchikan Salmon Walk to learn about the fish’s impact on the town (and maybe even spot some, in season, at the Salmon Ladder). The walk will take you past the Totem Heritage Center (also $6, or get a combo ticket to both museums for $9), with its collection of 19th-century totem poles rescued from nearby islands. If you’re feeling adventurous, you can skip the tour and head out to the Saxman Native Village on your own. It’s 2 miles south of Ketchikan, so it's walkable — but for a few bucks, you can take a city bus there instead. It costs just $5 to wander the park on your own and see the 25 replica totem poles, as well as Native carvers working on new poles using traditional techniques. Things to do in Icy Strait Point, Alaska, for free or cheap Icy Strait Point is a manufactured cruise port near the town of Hoonah. It was created to offer everything cruisers could possibly want in a port, so all the activities are planned to get you to part ways with your hard-earned cash. That said, there are still plenty of things to do in Icy Strait Point for free or cheap. A free gondola ride transports visitors from one cruise pier area to the other, but if the line is long or you’re afraid of heights, you can walk the same path on nature trails instead. Keep your eyes out for wildlife. The port has tons of beach access, so you can wander Icy Strait’s shores, stop for scenic photos and look for marine life free of charge. At the Hoonah Cannery building, you can browse the Hoonah Packing Co. Cannery Museum exhibits interspersed among the shops, or get tickets to the Native dance show for $20 per person at the on-site ticket booth. From the cannery, it’s a 1 1/2-mile (roughly 30-minute) walk to Hoonah, an actual town where many of Icy Strait Point’s workers live and home to Alaska's largest Tlingit village. You can also take an affordable $10 shuttle to town, where you can admire the totem poles and sip a local beer at Icy Strait Brewing. Things to do in Sitka, Alaska, for free or cheap Sitka offers a compelling mix of Native Alaskan and Russian history and culture, and a self-guided tour of the key sites in town won't cost you much (if anything at all). You can get a free tour of the Russian Bishop’s House, an example of 19th-century architecture during Russia’s colonization of Sitka. Baranof Castle State Historic Site (Castle Hill) was occupied throughout the centuries by Tlingit people and later by Russian settlers, and it was the site chosen for the transfer of Alaska from Russia to the U.S. You can check out the views and the informative signs for free. St. Michael Cathedral National Historic Landmark is an exact replica of the first Russian Orthodox church in the Americas. Because the site has an active congregation, visitors can view its collection of 17th-century religious artifacts for a limited time each day. Museums with small admission fees include the Sitka History Museum (featuring exhibits on local history) and the Sheldon Jackson Museum (showcasing a collection of Alaska Native artifacts). If exploring old cemeteries is your thing, you’ll want to stop at the more than 200-year-old Sitka Russian Cemetery, with gravestones made from the ballast of Russian ships. The Sitka National Historical Park’s visitor center and grounds (with walking trails and totem pole installations) are open to all, free of charge. It’s a scenic spot for an easy nature walk, or you can come inside to learn more about Sitka’s Russian and Tlingit cultures or join a ranger program. You don’t need a tour to gawk at eagles, hawks, owls and falcons at the Alaska Raptor Center. Admission is $16, though it is a bit of a walk from downtown. Watch injured birds relearn how to fly, and take a stroll through the center’s forested grounds. Finally, you can attend various dance performances at affordable ticket prices. The Alaska Storytellers dance show ($15) celebrates traditional and modern Russian dance, while the New Archangel Dancers' performances highlight Russian folk dances. Or, step into a Tlingit clan house to enjoy the music, costumes and choreography of the Naa Kahidi Tlingit Dancers. You don’t need to spend a fortune on tours to explore Alaska's culture and history or enjoy its natural splendor. You’ll find plenty of free things to do in port on an Alaska cruise. However, I do encourage you to budget for a few tours, whether it’s to travel beyond the port area into Alaska’s wilderness or to immerse yourself in an activity, such as dog sledding, kayaking, fishing, or whale or bear watching. You won’t regret spending the money on amazing experiences and memories. Planning a cruise? Start with these stories:

item.title: IDEA: Christmas lights London 2026: where to see the best displays
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Seeing the Christmas lights in London is high on the bucket list for all lovers of the festive season. Come mid-November, some of the world’s busiest shopping streets and neighbourhoods transform into winter wonderlands where hundreds of thousands of twinkling lights illuminate storefronts. Following the grand launch event that lures thousands of spectators in for an evening of entertainment, carols and treats, many remain until early January. Mulled wine and cider scent the air, stallholders sell unique gifts and glittering baubles beside street food vendors in Christmas markets and little ones emerge, beaming, from visits with Santa in snow-dusted dens. Here, we’ve rounded up all the London Christmas lights worth seeing, plus the latest information and when to expect the grand reveal. If you're seeking more festive inspiration in the capital, check out our guide to the best Christmas events in London. When do Christmas lights in London start? Christmas lights in London start turning on in early to mid-November. All of the key attractions and streets are illuminated by the last week of the month. Most major light switch-ons are scheduled for different days, so there's a chance to attend more than one festive evening if you're in town. When do Christmas lights in London end? The Christmas lights are taken down in the first week of January. However, lights may stay around longer if they're part of a winter exhibition or showcase. Look up to the heavens between splurges in the flagship stores dotted along Regent Street, and you'll see more than 300,000 glittering LED lights. The Spirit of Christmas display that has captivated shoppers for more than a decade returns for another outing, marking a beloved sign that the festivities are upon us. The switch-on event sees the iconic street cleared of traffic between 5pm and 9pm on the 5 November; the team are being tight-lipped, we expect there to be plenty of surprises on the night and beyond. Steady yourselves, Potterheads – the boy wizard’s adventures are set to play out along Europe’s busiest shopping street. For its dazzling 2026 display, Oxford Street has partnered with HBO Max, home of the new Harry Potter series, to transform this corner of the capital into a spellbinding wizarding world. There’s plenty of magical action to be had thanks to the opening of the UK’s largest official Harry Potter Shop on 134-140 Oxford Street. Step inside the two-storey space inspired by Diagon Alley and sense the nostalgia racing back. Christmas is getting ‘remixed’ across King’s Cross and Coal Drops Yard this festive season, as the area reimagines age-old traditions with a jam-packed programme between the end of November and the start of January. There’s a roller rink soundtracked by feel-good festive hits and dancefloor classics, and the winter market runs throughout the season – while the usual 100-odd restaurants and stores are cosy havens as the temperatures dip. It’s a Very Merry Marylebone Christmas in W1, as one of central London’s most charming corners is illuminated from mid-November onwards. The switch-on event is a festive highlight to pop in the diary, as Marylebone Village is transformed into a winter wonderland packed with curated stalls, a variety of food and drink offerings, family-friendly entertainment and a spectacular 55-foot Ferris wheel. BBC broadcaster and local resident Jo Good hosts an afternoon of live performances on Devonshire Street before the 6pm switch-on led by an as-yet-unannounced celebrity guest. Long regarded as one of the capital’s most festive spots from mid-November onwards, Covent Garden’s seasonal spectacular is especially befitting of its West End location. The Theatre of Christmas sees Londoners and visiting Chrimbo-lovers invited onto the piazza for a jam-packed, seven-week programme of events celebrating the area’s rich heritage of performance. The 12 November switch-on sees the 50-foot Christmas tree, decked with giant bells, baubles and over 300,000 lights, come to life as West End casts lead the entertainment. Elsewhere, brand-new installation The Forest of Theatre features trees inspired by some of the most iconic productions, while snowfall is guaranteed every hour from midday to 9pm from 4 December. Don’t miss the annual winter light trail at Kew's Royal Botanic Gardens, which illuminates the grounds over the festive period. Wander through the twinkling light tunnels, watch as the water features sparkle and be dazzled by the magical colours flooding the trees, all before catching the mesmerising display at Palm House. Pay a visit to Father Christmas and warm up with a hot spiced cider or hot chocolate for the ultimate winter evening out. New for 2026 are adults-only nights on the 3 and 9 December. Ludgate Circus becomes a winter wonderland following the mid-November switch-on as the ‘Festive Fleet Street Quarter’ returns. The display is bigger, better and brighter this year, thanks to a larger lighting display sparkling through the season, following a launch celebration promising festive fun for all with games, food and live music. Following the success of 2025’s Snoopy in The City sculpture trail, the team at Fleet Street Quarter have called on Dennis the Menace and his trusty Gnasher to launch the Mega Mischief Trail. Until 15 January, embark on the ultimate Beano expedition and celebrate 75 years of Dennis by following a route of a dozen artist-designed installations. The lively lighting ceremony of central London’s show-stopping Christmas tree dates back to 1947. The towering Norwegian spruce is a gift from Norway to London, thanks to British support during World War II. The tree is always decorated in traditional Norwegian style, with distinctive strings of vertical lights, while energy-efficient bulbs (and a stringent tree-recycling programme) help keep things sustainable. London’s trendiest shopping street asks us to Press Play on Christmas on 4 November. For 2026, Carnaby Street draws inspiration from the colour, confidence and energy of a British 90s Christmas, taking many of us back in time on a nostalgic, snow-dusted adventure. Sign up to receive the This is Soho newsletter and unlock a host of exclusive on-the-night offers – plus a complimentary cocktail or soft drink from 4pm on the night of the switch-on (applied to the first 1,000 redemptions). The Lord Mayor of London kickstarts Christmas in the City of London at Leadenhall Market’s annual switch-on spectacular, complete with pyrotechnic firework fountains and the unveiling of the 26-foot Christmas tree. Make a festive visit to the market and embark on a guided walk as local experts tell tales of Leadenhall Market's past and present. For the past few years, Savile Row's Christmas lights have been inspired by the tools found in every tailor's workshop – fitting for the UK's leading tailoring district. These include giant illuminated golden shears cutting through a glittering swathe of ‘fabric’, with the message of ‘Savile Row Christmas’ twinkling against the night sky. In terms of sustainability credentials, the displays are composed of more than 5,000 extra-low-energy bulbs, while elements of the decorations are 3D printed from 100 per cent recyclable plastic. St Katharine Docks is set to twinkle from 19 November, when a Christmas market opens up at 5pm and invites Londoners in for an evening of yuletide fun beside the historic Dickens Inn Pub. Expect an appearance from the Yeomen Warders of the Tower of London at 5.45pm, before Santa arrives ahead of the 7pm switch-on and musical finale. If you can’t make the main event, head to the docks between 7 November and 3 January to see the Christmas market (Monday - Sunday, 11am - 8pm). Old Spitalfields Market may be home to some of the most underrated Christmas lights in London, as the marketplace is illuminated by baubles, wreaths and glittering lights throughout the season. The family-friendly switch-on takes place on 11 November this year, with performances from 4pm, festive tunes from the House of Le Touche Gospel Choir at 5.30pm and the grand reveal at 6pm – all fuelled with plenty of mulled wine and mince pies, of course.

item.title: United is bringing its nicest plane (with the Polaris Studios) to a city that never sees it
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
United Airlines is bringing its most premium plane to a city where it’s rarely spotted. In January, the Chicago-based carrier will operate a few round trips between Las Vegas and Tokyo, and TPG has learned United plans to use one of its brand-new, luxe Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners on the route. This is the posh plane United debuted earlier this year, featuring the “Elevated” interior, complete with its next-generation Polaris Suites and the extra-spacious Polaris Studios. To score a seat on one of those aircraft, you typically have to be flying out of one of United’s major hubs like San Francisco or Houston. So far, the carrier has prioritized these planes — which have a whopping 99 premium seats — on routes to destinations where high-end seats are in high demand, like London, Singapore and Seoul. But it will make a limited appearance on a route United doesn’t typically fly: Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) in Las Vegas to Narita International Airport (NRT) in Tokyo. The occasion for the special route with the luxe plane is the 2027 Consumer Electronics Show, which is set to run in Vegas from Jan. 6 to Jan. 9. It’s one of the biggest conventions in the city each year, which draws visitors from all over the world. Airlines often add special temporary routes around major events — sometimes with planes fit for the occasion, such as when American Airlines sent its popular Airbus “A321T” to Sin City for the Super Bowl in 2024. We also noted last month how carriers are leaning more heavily into major sporting events, with new and unusual routes focused on college and professional football games. United’s 787 will certainly be a unique sight at LAS, but top rival Delta Air Lines is the U.S. airline that has historically made the biggest splash at CES. Nearly four years ago, at that convention, Delta laid out its plans to make on-board Wi-Fi free for all SkyMiles members — a move that nearly every major U.S. carrier matched. And in January 2025, Delta took over Vegas’ iconic Sphere for a keynote presentation by its CEO, Ed Bastian. Delta, for its part, is also adding special routes centered around CES. It’ll operate one-off services from Las Vegas to Hong Kong and Taipei, along with extra daily flights during the event to its hubs and its focus city, Austin. Route Details: United’s CES 2027 flights As for United, its “Elevated” 787 service from LAS to NRT will run on three days toward the tail-end of CES: Jan. 9, 10 and 11. United’s premium-configured 787-9 features: - 56 standard Polaris business-class suites - 123 seats in the main cabin, including 33 extra legroom Economy Plus seats Flights from Tokyo to Las Vegas (Jan. 3, 4 and 5) will be on an older Boeing 777-200ER. item.title: INSTRUCTION: Hertz President’s Circle elite status is included with several top travel cards. I put it to the test to see if it delivers real value
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
In all that time, I never once bothered to activate one of its perks: the complimentary Hertz President's Circle status. President's Circle is the top published tier of the Hertz Gold+ loyalty program, and earning it the traditional way means completing 15 rentals or spending $3,000 with Hertz in a calendar year. The reason I overlooked it is that I rent a car maybe a couple of times a year and usually shop around for the best deal, with little brand loyalty. But with a full day ahead of me recently to explore the spectacular Rocky Mountain National Park in Colorado, I wanted to put this elite status to the test to see whether it was a valuable credit card benefit. What is Hertz President's Circle? President's Circle is the highest published elite tier in Hertz Gold+ Rewards, the rental company's loyalty program, which costs nothing to join. It sits above the entry-level Gold tier and the mid-tier Five Star elite status. President's Circle members receive: - A guaranteed one-car-class upgrade at participating locations, with a maximum upgrade to a full-size car - The widest selection of vehicles at Hertz Ultimate Choice locations, where you can choose any car in the President's Circle section - The ability to skip the counter at select locations - 1.5 Hertz Gold+ Rewards points per dollar spent on qualifying base rental charges, a 50% bonus over the base earning rate - No additional driver fee for a spouse or domestic partner who has a credit card in their own name and meets Hertz's standard rental qualifications - A dedicated President's Circle customer service line It's worth remembering that Ultimate Choice is available only at select Hertz airport locations, and you'll need to reserve a midsize or larger vehicle. The guaranteed upgrade requires a reservation made at least 48 hours in advance at a participating location, is capped at a full-size vehicle and does not apply to Manager's Special rentals or certain premium vehicle collections. Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note, enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold Plus Rewards enrollment process (e.g. at Hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply. The following premium credit cards offer complimentary President's Circle status: - American Express Platinum Card® and The Business Platinum Card® from American Express: Enrollment is required; terms apply. U.S. consumer and business Platinum cardmembers who enrolled before July 9, 2026, must re-enroll through the Car Rental Privileges tile in their Amex benefits by Dec. 31, 2026. Allow up to 72 hours for processing. - Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card and Capital One Venture X Business: Enrollment is required through the benefits tab of their Capital One account on the Capital One website or mobile app. Eligible cardholders can also enroll authorized users through this process. Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note that enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold+ enrollment process (e.g., at hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program, and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply. - Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card or the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve Business American Express Card: Enrollment is required; terms apply. Basic cardmembers must add their U.S. Hertz Gold+ account number to the Other Loyalty Programs section of their SkyMiles profile, then enroll on Delta's Hertz promotion page. Delta says the status can take up to eight weeks to appear in your Hertz account, so this isn't one to leave until the week before a trip. Delta SkyMiles Platinum Medallion and Diamond Medallion elite members are eligible for complimentary Hertz President's Circle status following this same process. How to make a President's Circle booking To receive the President's Circle status benefits, it's important to follow the correct booking process, which is not onerous: - Join Hertz Gold+ if you aren’t already a member, as every route to complimentary President’s Circle status requires it. - Enroll through the specific card issuer or Delta process described above rather than relying on Hertz's standard enrollment page to recognize your eligibility. - Check that the President’s Circle status shows in your Hertz account before you make a reservation. - Make sure your driver’s license details are saved in your Hertz profile so you’re set up to skip the counter. - Book a midsize car or larger at a location with Ultimate Choice, which mostly means airport locations. - At pickup, look for your name on the President’s Circle board and, if you need help, head to the Five Star and President’s Circle desk rather than the main counter. The President's Circle benefits I actually received As a solo driver, there was no need for me to add a complimentary second driver, and I didn't need to call Hertz in advance, so I couldn't test the dedicated President's Circle line. I received 1.5 Hertz Gold+ Rewards points per dollar spent on the rental, as advertised, but the real perks I was interested in were the pickup experience and the type of car I received. When I arrived at the pickup location, my name was on the President's Circle board with a note to "see desk." This was my first Hertz Gold+ rental, and first-time members may need to verify their driver's license and payment card at the Gold desk before they can bypass the counter on subsequent rentals. Make sure you go to the Five Star/President's Circle desk, rather than the main building desk. At larger locations like Denver International Airport (DEN), where I was, these are two separate buildings. Being unsure, I went to the main building desk and had an utterly bizarre interaction with the staff there, who found my reservation, insisted my President's Circle status had expired, despite me only activating it a month earlier, refused to activate it and insisted that if I reactivated myself, I would have to cancel the booking and rebook if I wanted any status benefits, which would likely be much more expensive to do last minute. This is despite my showing them my live Hertz account, including the booking confirmation, and my President's Circle status level was clearly visible. Fortunately, I sought a second opinion at the Five Star and President's Circle desk, where the staff could not have been more helpful, found my reservation, could immediately see my President's Circle status and had me on my way to the President's Circle lot within minutes. Choosing my car from the President's Circle section This was the highlight of the day. More than 50 cars were waiting in the President's Circle section. I don't pretend to be an expert on cars (I don't currently own one), so I just chose the one that looked the most luxurious. Walking up and down the rows and picking out exactly what I wanted to drive was great fun, and I settled on a shiny new 2026 Wrangler Sahara 4WD with just a few thousand miles on the clock, which I thought would be awesome for tackling the winding roads of the Rocky Mountain National Park. Having originally booked a midsize-category Kia K4, driving off the lot in a Jeep Wrangler Sahara sure felt like a superior car, but I subsequently checked the sticker price for each car, new. At more than twice the Kia's retail price, the Jeep was definitely an upgrade. With the keys already inside, I drove my chosen car to the exit, showed the attendant my receipt with the large "PC" status written on it and headed out the exit to the mountains. After years of ignoring the Hertz President’s Circle status that comes with my Venture X card, I’m a little sheepish about not using it sooner. Despite the initial confusion at the main counter, Hertz ultimately delivered on the status benefits I valued most, and for someone who doesn't know much about cars, I felt like a television game show winner, wandering the lot and choosing any car I wished. The rental wasn't the cheapest from any agency in the area, so if an upgrade doesn't interest you, you still may wish to shop around. Ultimate Choice is available only at certain locations, so a downtown Hertz branch may not have a President's Circle section at all. It’s probably not a perk I’d open a new credit card for on its own, but if you already hold one of the cards above, submitting the enrollment only takes a few minutes, and it turned what would have been a forgettable rental into one of the highlights of my trip. For special occasions like exploring one of the country's best national parks, I would definitely give my President's Circle status a spin again.

item.title: Why Germans won't buy a round of beer
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
'People will be counting': What a German expert wants you to know about buying drinks in Germany From Berlin bars to Bavarian beer gardens, who pays for what is taken seriously in Germany. Here's why splitting the bill can actually be a sign of friendship. Picture the scene: you're travelling through Germany and have gone out to dinner with a new group of local friends. Everyone has eaten, had a drink or two and shared plenty of laughs. Then the bill arrives. There is no "let's just split it". Instead, the first person tells the waiter exactly what they ordered – spaghetti and two beers – and pays precisely that amount. The next pays for their pizza and glass of wine. And so it goes, right around the table. Ute Junker is an award-winning journalist who was born in Australia to German parents and went to school in both countries. She has edited magazines in both Australia and Germany and writes frequently about German culture and history. Welcome to Germany, a country that celebrates precision, even among friends enjoying an evening out. Splitting the bill evenly is not an idea that has taken off here. Nor is buying each other rounds the same generous gesture it is in other countries. For visitors accustomed to everyone paying an equal share – or taking tuns at the bar – this item-by-item accounting can feel strangely formal. And in a country with such a celebrated beer culture, it raises an obvious question: why don't Germans buy each other drinks? This unspoken rule applies even in the most casual situations. In carefree Berlin, summer evenings often see younger people skipping a night of bar hopping in favour of gathering outside a Späti (late-night convenience store). Even when one person heads inside to buy the next round of drinks, don't assume generosity has replaced arithmetic. "People will be counting who has paid how many rounds, most definitely," says Julian Berger, bartender at Orania Berlin, a luxury hotel in the city's edgy Kreuzberg district. Dr Harald Pitters, an Austrian trend researcher who is married to a German, says the instinct is rooted in fairness and a desire to keep control of the situation. He has also seen how uncertainty can make buying rounds uncomfortable. "Two of my best friends are German, and this was always a point of contention when we went out together," he says. "They didn't like the idea of rounds when there was no certainty around how long we would stay and how many rounds we would have. If everyone pays their way there is no room for disappointment." "Germans have a very strong sense of justice," Berger adds. "They feel more comfortable if everyone pays for themselves. They don't like it when there is an imbalance." In other words, keeping the bill clear is not necessarily seen as ungenerous. It can be a way of protecting the friendship. There is even a German saying that sums up this mentality: "Klare Rechnung, gute Freunde" (clear accounts, good friends). As with any practice, however, there are exceptions to the rule. In the Biergärten (beer gardens) in southern Germany, where the standard drink is a one-litre mug of beer, rounds are more common. In fact, it is in the country's more traditional areas, including Bavaria, that you are more likely to see friends buying drinks for each other. This is particularly true at traditional community festivals, which Pittars says are enjoying a revival among young people. "At an Erntedankfest [harvest festival, where beer is the standard drink], it is very usual to buy rounds. You would out yourself as very uptight if you just bought a drink for you and your partner," he says. "That also applies at Karneval [Carnival] in Cologne or Hafengeburtstag [Port Anniversary] in Hamburg – any communal event involving drinking and dancing." So what should visitors do? Berger advises assuming that everyone will pay their own way – unless someone makes it clear otherwise. "If you are out with someone and they say, "Ich lade dich ein" [I am inviting you], that means they are paying," he says. And there is no need to feel awkward about asking the waiter to split the bill, either. Most will automatically ask, "Getrennt oder zusammen?" (separately or together). For many Germans, the natural answer remains: "Getrennt, bitte" (separately, please). – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: A sky-high Vegas bar, a chic new Marriott in South Africa and more hotel news
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Here in New York City, it's one of the absolute best weekends of the year: Halloween and the New York City Marathon. Last year, a team of TPG staff came out to the race to cheer me on while I ran, which was a very caring way for my work family to spend their free time. And speaking of free time, Club Med recently commissioned a study of 2,000 Americans and Canadians to find how people actually feel about their free time — and what they do with it. One statistic in the report really resonated with me: 81% of North Americans miss the sense of wonder they had as kids more than the free time they had then. So this week I'm sharing some hotel news that speaks to that sense of wonder we all apparently long for, like a chic new hotel at the very tip of Africa to a revamped, sky-high cocktail bar with views of the iconic Las Vegas strip. Here's the hotel news you need to know about. One of the most anticipated hotel openings of the year, The Cape Town Edition, is now open. Set on the V&A Waterfront, the stylish hotel is the brand's first outpost in Africa. At the property, guests can stay in one of 142 rooms and suites, enjoy art and design selected as "a reflection of Africa's creative landscape," and eat at numerous dining and bar outlets. And for people like me who love to relax, the hotel has a spa. One of New York's most famous hotels is getting a spa In November, New York's celebrity-loved hotel The Mark is getting its first spa: The Mark Wellness & Longevity Spa by Augustinus Bader. The Mark is already The Met Gala's fashion hot spot, plus home to caviar-loaded baked potatoes at Caviar Kaspia, so it only makes sense to have a luxe spa. The spa, the first Augustinus Bader-branded location in the U.S., will feature three treatment rooms, state-of-the-art and science-backed treatments, plus in-room massage services. The opening comes hot on the heels of The Mark's recent room updates, making the hotel as fresh — and relaxing — as ever. W Las Vegas revamps and reopens a dreamy rooftop bar In 2024, Marriott took over the former Delano hotel at Mandalay Bay and converted it into the W Las Vegas. Now, two years later, the W brand is really making the hotel its own with the relaunch of Skyfall Rooftop Bar & Lounge. Situated on the 64th floor and offering panoramic views of Sin City, Rockwell Group recreated the space with bold interiors accenting the floor-to-ceiling windows. In the hotel's lobby, the Living Room bar has also been reimagined. "Together, these spaces sophisticatedly blend glamour, futuristic energy, and immersive nightlife to capture the true spirit of Las Vegas while embodying the bold, playful quality signature to a W hotel," W Las Vegas said in a statement shared with TPG. This Delaware hotel wants you to embrace the 'Year of the Horse' — literally Going back to how we spend our free time, Club Med's report also shared that 88% of people experienced at least one positive impact the last time they challenged themselves to try something new. If you want to feel that positive impact, it might be time to go ... to Delaware. Hotel Du Pont in Wilmington has launched the Equestrian Escape Package, which comes with equestrian-centric loaner pieces, like riding boots and jackets, from The Frye Company; a private riding lesson at the 200-acre Carousel Park Equestrian Center; and a gourmet picnic from the hotel's Le Cavalier French brasserie. We've all been patiently waiting for the 69-room Thompson Rome, the first property from the brand in Italy, to open its doors. Well, that day has finally come. The hotel, right near Piazza Venezia and other major attractions, features restored elements from the hotel's original building, a contemporary Mediterranean restaurant, a rooftop cocktail bar and a lobby bar.
